source: Cornell University LIHREC Vegetable MD Online / UMass Amherst Extension Cucurbit IPM Program
title: Squash and Pumpkin Powdery Mildew (Podosphaera xanthii, Golovinomyces orontii)
content: Powdery mildew is the most common, most widely distributed, and most consistently observed foliar disease of all cucurbit crops worldwide, affecting summer squash (Cucurbita pepo L. var. melopepo: zucchini, yellow straightneck, yellow crookneck, pattypan, scallop), winter squash (C. moschata Duch., C. maxima Duch. ex Lam.: butternut, acorn, Hubbard, kabocha, kuri, delicata, spaghetti), pumpkin (C. pepo, C. maxima, C. argyrosperma), cucumber (Cucumis sativus), melon (Cucumis melo), watermelon (Citrullus lanatus), and gourds. The primary causal organism on squash and pumpkin worldwide is the obligate biotrophic ascomycete Podosphaera xanthii (Castagne) U. Braun & Shishkoff [formerly known as Sphaerotheca fuliginea (Schltdl.) Pollacci; anamorphic stage: Oidium subgenus Fibroidium]. A second powdery mildew fungus, Golovinomyces orontii (Castagne) V.P. Heluta [formerly Erysiphe cichoracearum DC. var. cichoracearum; anamorph: Oidium subgenus Reticuloidium], also occurs on cucurbits but is generally of minor importance on squash and pumpkin compared to cucumber and greenhouse melons. P. xanthii is the predominant species in open-field commercial production of all warm-season cucurbits in North America, Central America, the Caribbean, South America, Africa, the Middle East, India, China, Japan, and Australia; G. orontii is more common in cool-temperate greenhouses, high tunnels, and on autumn-grown cucurbits in northern Europe, Canada, and the northwestern US. Powdery mildew reduces squash and pumpkin yields by 20-50% annually in unprotected susceptible cultivars through reduced photosynthetic leaf area, premature chlorosis and defoliation, reduced fruit size and number, sunscald of exposed fruit, and incomplete fruit color development in C. maxima and C. moschata winter squashes; severe epidemics on summer squash (zucchini, yellow squash) can reduce marketable fruit yield by > 70% due to cessation of vine growth and poor fruit set from pollen viability loss on heavily infected staminate flowers. The first symptoms of powdery mildew on squash and pumpkin appear on the oldest (lowest, basal) leaves near the crown of the vine approximately 3-6 weeks after transplanting or direct seeding: faint, chlorotic yellow-green mottling and blistering (chlorotic blotches) on the upper surface of mature, fully expanded leaves. Within 3-5 days, a thin, superficial, talcum-like, white, powdery ectophytic growth of mycelium, conidiophores, and catenulate (in chains) single-celled, hyaline, barrel-shaped conidia (25-45 x 14-22 um) develops first on the LOWER (abaxial) leaf surface directly beneath the upper-surface chlorotic blotches; subsequently, the white powdery growth spreads to cover both surfaces of infected leaves, petioles, young vine stems, peduncles (fruit stalks), and occasionally the skin of young developing winter squash fruit. In severe infections, entire leaves become covered in a thick, white to slightly grayish felt-like layer of mycelium and conidia; infected leaves gradually turn bright yellow, then brown (necrotic), wither, become brittle, and die prematurely 2-3 weeks after initial infection. Heavily infected summer squash vines (zucchini, yellow crookneck) cease producing new female flowers and young fruit within 10-14 days of the first symptoms on the crown leaves, causing a complete 'cutoff' of marketable yields. On the thick, succulent stems of C. maxima 'Hubbard', 'Atlantic Giant', and 'Kabocha' pumpkin and squash, powdery mildew produces dark, purplish-gray to brown, rough, corky, superficial stem lesions (called 'powdery mildew stem scab') in late autumn, which are overwintering sites of the sexual cleistothecial fruiting bodies. Unlike the downy mildews, cucurbit powdery mildews do NOT require free moisture on the leaf surface for infection; in fact, conidial germination is actually inhibited by free-standing water films on the leaf. The optimum conditions for infection, colonization, and secondary spread are moderate temperatures (20-27 C / 68-81 F), moderate to high atmospheric relative humidity (50-90% RH; optimum 65-75% RH for maximum conidial production), and dense, shaded, poorly ventilated vine canopies; conidial germination and infection are reduced sharply at temperatures below 10 C and above 35 C, and at RH < 40%. The disease develops first in the lower, shaded, inner canopy of the squash vine where air movement is poor and humidity is stable, then spreads progressively outward to newer leaves and upward through the canopy as the season progresses. P. xanthii is polycyclic, producing successive asexual spore crops every 5-10 days throughout the growing season. Long-distance spread of P. xanthii occurs via wind-dispersed conidia which are easily carried 50-500 km in turbulent atmospheric flow from southern, earlier-planted cucurbit fields northward during the spring and summer; in many temperate areas (northern US, Canada, northern Europe), the pathogen does not survive winter conditions locally and each new growing season's powdery mildew epidemic is initiated by wind-blown conidia arriving from more southerly latitudes. Where winter temperatures permit survival (USDA plant hardiness zones 6b and warmer), P. xanthii also overwinters as melanized, globose, sexual fruiting bodies called chasmothecia (formerly cleistothecia; 85-120 um diameter) on old infected cucurbit crop debris (vine stems, leaf petioles). Each chasmothecium develops characteristic dichotomously branched (mycelioid) appendages and contains a single ascus with 8 ellipsoidal ascospores; in the following spring, chasmothecia absorb moisture during rainfall events and crack open, forcibly discharging ascospores that serve as an additional source of local primary inoculum. Management of cucurbit powdery mildew on squash and pumpkin requires an integrated program combining genetic resistance, cultural practices, forecasting models, and fungicide applications with strict FRAC resistance management. (1) Genetic resistance is the most economically effective control measure. Three classes of powdery mildew resistance have been bred into squash and pumpkin: (a) qualitative major race-specific Pm genes (Pm-0, Pm-1, Pm-2, Pm-3, Pm-4, Pm-5 derived from C. pepo ssp. ovifera and C. lundelliana): these provide high-level immunity against specific P. xanthii physiological races but are frequently overcome by new virulent races within 3-6 years of commercial deployment. (b) polygenic, quantitative, partial, horizontal, adult-plant field resistance derived from C. moschata 'Nigerian Local' and C. okeechobeensis subsp. martinezii: this provides moderate but highly durable, race-nonspecific protection against all P. xanthii races and is the preferred type of resistance for commercial modern F1 hybrid squash and pumpkin cultivars. (c) powdery mildew tolerance: some older C. maxima and C. moschata open-pollinated cultivars (e.g., 'Butternut 86', 'Waltham Butternut Improved', 'Seminole Pumpkin', 'Long Island Cheese') tolerate heavy powdery mildew infection without significant yield loss due to vigorous vine growth and photosynthetic compensation from newer leaves. A large percentage of modern F1 hybrid summer squash (zucchini, yellow squash), pumpkin, and winter squash cultivars currently carry one or both classes of resistance; examples include 'Paycheck PM/WSQR' (zucchini), 'Success PM' (straightneck yellow), 'Sunburst PM' (pattypan), 'Waltham Butternut Supreme PM' (butternut), 'Hallow PM' (jack-o'-lantern pumpkin), 'Racer PM' (processing pumpkin), 'Cinnamon Girl PM' (acorn), 'Gold Nugget PM' (kabocha). (2) Cultural practices: (a) avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which promotes overly lush, shaded, succulent vine growth that is highly susceptible to powdery mildew. (b) plant cucurbits in fields with full sun exposure, wide inter-row spacing (1.5-2.5 m between rows depending on vine type), and trellising of vining C. pepo summer squash where practical to improve air movement, increase sun exposure, and reduce canopy humidity. (c) remove and destroy the first 2-3 heavily infected crown leaves when symptoms are first observed at the start of the epidemic to reduce initial inoculum. (d) manage weeds (especially pigweed, lambsquarters, ground cherry, milkweed, common mallow) in field borders, as some wild weed species serve as local green-bridge hosts for P. xanthii between cucurbit plantings. (e) in high-tunnel and greenhouse production, use horizontal airflow (HAF) fans to keep canopy RH < 80%, vent aggressively, heat at night to reduce condensation, and use UV-transparent greenhouse covering plastics where pollinator safety permits (UVB radiation strongly reduces P. xanthii spore viability). (3) Forecasting and disease-warning models (Cucurbit Powdery Mildew Forecaster, VegEdge, CU-PM, Ag-Radar) schedule the first powdery mildew spray based on accumulated degree-days (base 50 F) after planting, historical first-detection dates, and regional reports of powdery mildew incidence from sentinel scouting plots, typically reducing total seasonal fungicide use by 25-40% compared to rigid calendar-based weekly sprays. (4) Chemical and biorational fungicide programs are the standard management tool for high-value commercial summer squash and pumpkin production. P. xanthii is infamous for developing extremely rapid resistance to single-site fungicide modes of action: > 30 different fungicide FRAC groups have been registered for cucurbit powdery mildew worldwide since the 1960s, and P. xanthii field populations have developed documented resistance to 22 of those groups including FRAC 1 (MBC / benomyl), FRAC 2 (dicarboximide), FRAC 3 (DMI triazoles - widespread reduced-sensitivity populations exist globally since the 1990s), FRAC 11 (QoI / strobilurins - widespread resistance since 1999), FRAC 9 (AP / cyprodinil), FRAC U6 (fluopyram - resistance detected in NY and FL since 2020), FRAC 50 (metrafenone), FRAC 13 (azafenidin), and FRAC U8 (cyflufenamid). Strict FRAC anti-resistance guidelines are therefore MANDATORY for sustainable powdery mildew control: (a) NEVER use any single-site fungicide SOLO (alone) for powdery mildew; always tank-mix with a full rate of a multi-site contact partner (FRAC M2 sulfur, FRAC M3 mancozeb, FRAC M1 copper, potassium bicarbonate, mineral oil). (b) Limit maximum 2-3 consecutive applications of the same FRAC mode-of-action group, then switch to a completely different FRAC group. (c) Do not make more than 4-5 total seasonal applications of any high-resistance-risk FRAC group. (d) Initiate sprays at the first sign of 1% disease incidence on lower canopy leaves (do not wait for heavy sporulation - protectant programs are far more effective than curative). Most effective current FRAC groups against cucurbit powdery mildew (based on Cornell LIHREC, Penn State, UMass, and University of Florida trial data 2019-2024): FRAC M2 SULFUR (micronized wettable sulfur, dusting sulfur, flowable sulfur; the oldest and still one of the most effective multi-site protectants with ZERO documented P. xanthii resistance after > 160 years of use; excellent as a standalone protectant or tank-mix partner in all programs; note: do not apply sulfur to cucurbits when air temperature > 90 F / 32 C to avoid phytotoxic fruit russeting and leaf necrosis; sulfur is OMRI-listed for organic production). FRAC 3 DMI (myclobutanil, tebuconazole, difenoconazole, prothioconazole, metconazole, triflumizole - still provide 50-80% control on many moderately resistant P. xanthii populations when tank-mixed with sulfur; use high labeled rates). FRAC 7 SDHI (fluxapyroxad, boscalid, penthiopyrad, benzovindiflupyr, pydiflumetofen, isofetamid, fluopyram; currently the most effective single-site group; FRAC 7 + FRAC 11 premixes are industry standard for conventional cucurbit programs). FRAC 11 QoI (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, trifloxystrobin, kresoxim-methyl; protectant only; do not use solo because of widespread QoI resistance in most P. xanthii populations; always tank-mix with full-rate sulfur or mancozeb). FRAC 50 (metrafenone, cyflufenamid - excellent protectant + mild systemic kickback; still highly effective in most regions where not heavily used previously). FRAC VPH (horticultural mineral oils, Supreme 435, JMS Stylet-Oil, Omni Supreme; multi-site physical suffocation mode of action; 0 resistance risk; excellent translaminar activity; acceptable on squash and pumpkin when applied in cool early morning; do not tank-mix with sulfur, copper, or captan to avoid phytotoxicity; 7-day minimum reapplication interval). FRAC GB05 / bicarbonates (potassium bicarbonate, sodium bicarbonate, potassium carbonate; physical disruption of the ectophytic mycelium by osmotic lysis; 0 resistance risk; OMRI-listed organic option when combined with a nonionic spreader-sticker). In organic production, the standard effective program is a 7-10 day rotational schedule alternating between: (i) micronized wettable sulfur (2-4 lb/100 gal) + spreader-sticker, (ii) potassium bicarbonate (3-4 lb/100 gal) + JMS Stylet-Oil mineral oil (1-2% v/v) on a separate week, (iii) Bacillus amyloliquefaciens QST 713 / Serenade ASO (Serenade Maximum) or B. subtilis GB03 / Kodiak, (iv) Reynoutria sachalinensis giant knotweed extract (Regalia Maxx) + Bacillus pumilus QST 2808 (Sonata ASO), (v) Ampelomyces quisqualis AQ10 hyperparasitic fungus (applied pre-symptomatically for best results), (vi) Pseudozyma flocculosa (Sporodex L) yeast-like epiphyte. Organic programs correctly implementing these biorational materials on a strict 7-day protectant schedule achieve 60-80% powdery mildew reduction compared to untreated controls, approaching the performance of the best conventional programs under moderate disease pressure. (5) Squash and pumpkin harvested fruit post-harvest handling: fruit harvested from fields with severe powdery mildew vine infection should be washed with chlorinated water (50-100 ppm free chlorine, pH 6.5-7.5) + 0.1% potassium sorbate dip (2 minutes) to remove superficial powdery mildew mycelium from fruit surfaces and prevent post-harvest skin blemishes and peduncle rot during storage and shipment; C. maxima Hubbard, Banana, and Kabocha squash cure best at 27-29 C / 80-85 F and 80-85% RH for 10-14 days after harvest to promote wound periderm formation.
